title: Remember you will die
hook: tradition says monks kept skulls on their desks to value each day

segments.voice: Yesterday, hope written from chains: he which hath begun a good work will perform it. Your line was he will finish it. What had already begun, beside your fear? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

A skull on a writing desk, beside the candle and the open book. Tradition says some monks kept one there, not to be gloomy, but to be reminded. In old paintings a skull sometimes sits next to a saint at prayer, as calm as an inkwell. It's a strange thing to keep within reach. But the Bible has a prayer that asks for the same reminder, without any bones on the desk. Its heading calls it "A Prayer of Moses the man of God." Today's word is a Latin phrase for what the skull was saying, and the psalm has its own way of saying it.

First, the request. Psalm ninety, verse twelve: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Not count your years. Number your days. And it's asked as a lesson, teach us, not handed down as a threat. The point of the counting is a wiser heart. Second, how short. The same psalm says people are like grass: "In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth." And: "we spend our years as a tale that is told." The letter of James asks it outright: "For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away." Third, the Latin. Memento mori: remember that you will die. Not a Bible verse, but a saying Christians kept close to the Bible's own words. Some churches put it in the body. On Ash Wednesday, in Catholic and some Protestant churches, a minister marks ashes on the forehead, sometimes with words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Other churches don't keep the day. Fourth, why anyone would want this. Ecclesiastes says it is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting, because the living will lay it to heart. Remembering the end sorts what matters from what doesn't. In this block it sits beside everything else: dust, and all things new. On the desk, the skull sat beside an open book.

Here's the practice: think of your own death, gently, for about a minute. If today is a hard day for that, or you're grieving, number one day instead: just this one. Settle, and breathe. Picture your life as a tale that is told, with an ending you don't know. Don't add details. Just let it be true. Then turn to today. It's one of a numbered set. Ask what would make it count: a call, an apology, an hour given to someone. If you pray, you can say the line from Psalm ninety, teach us to number our days. If you don't, just hold the day in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Memento mori. Latin: remember that you will die. Kept close to Psalm ninety's prayer, teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Your line: number your days. Tonight, before you sleep, name one thing that made today count, and one thing you'd do tomorrow if you knew the days were few. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday, Catholic and some Protestant churches mark ashes on the forehead, sometimes with the words 'remember that thou art dust'; some Christians also pray Psalm 90 at funerals or at the turn of the year.

fork.setup: you're a monk with a skull on your desk. a visitor asks why you keep it. what's it for, in this tradition?
options: to frighten the younger monks into behaving.
to remember you will die, and so number your days wisely.
to honor a famous saint's relic.
fork.reveal: a reminder, not a threat: "so teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

original.note: Latin: remember that you will die (literally, remember to die).

notes: Monks keeping skulls on desks is attributed to tradition; skulls beside saints 'in old paintings' (e.g. Saint Jerome) is a general art claim without a cited source. Confirm.

Ash Wednesday: 'Catholic and some Protestant churches' mark ashes; Orthodox churches begin Lent differently and are not named. The formula 'remember that thou art dust' in howItsDone is a description of the rite's words, not a quotation from a cited translation. Confirm.
Practice handles death gently with an opt-out for the grieving ('number one day instead'). Confirm tone.
Original note: 'remember to die' as the literal sense of memento mori. Confirm.

Editor: 'the psalm says it first' (a priority claim) became 'the psalm has its own way of saying it'; 'Christians keep this beside everything' (a sweeping claim) became a statement about this block; the closing uplift line about the last word was replaced with the concrete desk detail.
Audit 2026-10-02: Psalm 90 (title, 6, 9, 12), James 4:14, Genesis 3:19 and Ecclesiastes 7:2 checked; no change.
